question: How are Subagents in Claude Code most accurately defined?
options: Specialized AI assistants to which Claude Code can delegate tasks in an isolated context window, returning only a summary to the main thread
UI plugins used solely to change the colors of the Terminal window
An SQL database used to store user passwords and API keys
A feature that automatically shares your entire chat history to public GitHub
explanation: Subagents are specialized assistants delegated tasks by Claude Code (Parent Agent). Each subagent runs in an isolated context window, independently performs file reads/searches/tool calls, and returns only a concise summary to the main conversation.

question: What core problem occurs with the Main Context Window when you work long-term with Claude Code WITHOUT using Subagents?
options: Every tool call, read file content, and search result accumulates in the finite Main Context Window, causing it to fill up quickly and making Claude gradually lose track of earlier parts of the conversation
Claude Code will automatically wipe the computer's hard drive after every 10 messages
The Main Context Window does not support reading source code files written in Python
The main context window will automatically shrink to 10 tokens after 5 minutes
explanation: The space of the Main Context Window is finite. When all file reads, searches, and tool calls pile up here, the context becomes polluted (context pollution/rot), and as it fills up, Claude starts forgetting important information from the beginning of the conversation.

question: When Claude Code launches a new Subagent, what are the 2 core components that its initial context window receives?
options: 1) A Custom System Prompt from the configuration file defining the subagent's role/behavior, and 2) A Task Description written by the Parent Agent based on the user's request
1) 100% of the entire chat history from the start of the Main Conversation session, and 2) All files in the operating system directory
1) Chat history of all other sibling Subagents, and 2) The system password file
1) Only the user's name, and 2) A list of favorite websites in the browser
explanation: According to Chapter 1 documentation, each subagent starts in an isolated context with: (1) A custom system prompt from the configuration file defining its role & behavior, and (2) A task description written by the Parent Agent based on what you asked for.

question: After a Subagent completes a series of file reads, searches, and processing steps, what information is sent back to the Main Conversation?
options: Only a concise summary of the results is returned to the main conversation
The entire raw content of every file that the Subagent opened and read along the way
All system error logs and binary code of the invoked tools
No information is returned at all; the user must manually open the log file to read it
explanation: The greatest strength of a subagent is its 'one-way valve' mechanism: all intermediate steps (file reads, searches, tool calls) are kept isolated, and upon completion, only the summary returns to the Main Conversation.

question: How does Claude Code handle the detailed conversation and intermediate working steps of a Subagent (which are not brought back to the Main Context)?
options: Claude Code saves the rest of the Subagent's detailed conversation to a separate transcript file
Claude Code emails the entire log to the network administrator
Claude Code stuffs everything into the operating system's PATH environment variable
Claude Code directly overwrites the project's README.md file
explanation: Although only a summary returns to the Main Conversation, Claude Code still saves the full detailed conversation history of the subagent into a separate transcript file.

question: What is the main tradeoff when using a Subagent to keep the Main Context Window clean?
options: The main conversation does not see the detailed process/steps the Subagent took to reach its final conclusions
The Subagent is completely unable to read any files on the hard drive
When using a Subagent, the Main Agent is permanently locked and cannot chat with the user anymore
A Subagent always takes 100 times longer for any question under 5 words
explanation: In Chapter 1 ('Why Subagents Matter'), the documentation clearly states: 'The tradeoff is that your main conversation doesn't see how the subagent reached its conclusions' — the main thread receives a clean answer without seeing the intermediate journey the subagent took.

question: In the Chapter 1 Practical Example, when you want to find which file handles authentication in an unfamiliar codebase and have to read through 15 files to find it, what happens if you delegate this task to the `Explore` Subagent?
options: The Main Context Window only records the question and the summary answer — it does NOT store the contents of the 15 files read during the search
All 15 files are copied into the Main Context Window for the user to inspect line by line
The `Explore` Subagent automatically deletes the 14 unrelated files from the project's hard drive
The `Explore` Subagent refuses to run because it is only allowed to read a maximum of 2 files
explanation: When using the `Explore` subagent, it digs through the 15 files in its own isolated context and returns a focused answer. The Main Context Window only stores the question and the result summary, saving thousands of main context tokens.

question: Which 3 Built-in Subagents does Claude Code ship with out of the box?
options: General-purpose subagent, Explore, and Plan
Frontend-builder, Database-admin, and DevOps-deployer
Compiler, Debugger, and Package-manager
Git-pusher, Docker-runner, and Browser-scraper
explanation: According to the 'Built-in Subagents' section in Chapter 1, Claude Code ships with 3 built-in subagents: (1) General-purpose subagent, (2) Explore, and (3) Plan.

question: Among Claude Code's Built-in Subagents, what is the `Explore` subagent specifically designed for?
options: Fast searching and navigation of codebases
Automatically rewriting the entire Git history and force-pushing to the main branch
Executing database deletion scripts in the Production environment
Simultaneously editing 100 source code files without reading their contents
explanation: `Explore` is a built-in subagent specialized for fast searching and navigation in codebases (typically using read-only tools to maintain safety and high speed).

question: Which Built-in Subagent in Claude Code is designed for multi-step tasks that require BOTH exploration and action?
options: General-purpose subagent
Explore subagent
Plan subagent
Read-only subagent
explanation: The `General-purpose subagent` is a versatile subagent used for multi-step tasks that need to combine both exploration and execution/action.

question: When is the `Plan` Built-in Subagent used by Claude Code?
options: Used in plan mode to research and analyze the codebase before presenting a plan
Only used after the application has been successfully deployed to the cloud
Used to automatically pay monthly AWS service bills
Used to compile C++ source code into machine code
explanation: According to Chapter 1: The `Plan` subagent is used in `plan mode` to perform isolated codebase research and analysis before synthesizing and presenting a plan to the user.

question: Beyond Built-in Subagents, users can create `Custom Subagents` by customizing which core elements?
options: Customizing System Prompts and Tool Access to fit specific workflows
Modifying neural network weights on Anthropic's servers
Changing the TCP/IP protocol of the Windows operating system
Rewriting the Linux kernel compiler in assembly language
explanation: Custom Subagents allow you to define specialized assistants (code reviewer, test writer, documentation generator, etc.) with Custom System Prompts and Custom Tool Access.

question: What are the 3 Key Takeaways (benefits) that Subagents provide according to the summary at the end of Chapter 1?
options: 1) Break work into focused pieces, 2) Keep the Main Context Window clean by isolating intermediate work, 3) Bring back just the information needed as a concise summary
1) Increase physical RAM capacity, 2) Reduce hard drive usage, 3) Automatically upgrade Internet bandwidth speed
1) Completely eliminate the need for System Prompts, 2) Allow API calls without Internet, 3) Automatically fix hardware failures
1) Merge all files into a single file, 2) Save all search logs into the Main Context, 3) Completely disable tool permission checks
explanation: The 3 core benefits of Subagents in the Chapter 1 Key Takeaways are: (1) Break work into focused pieces, (2) Keep your main context window clean by isolating intermediate work, and (3) Bring back just the information you need as a concise summary.

question: When a Subagent is executing file read (`Read`) and search (`Grep`) commands, where do the outputs returned from those tools appear?
options: Completely inside that Subagent's own Context Window (and recorded in its own separate transcript file)
Inserted directly into the middle of the Main Context Window's chat history immediately
Written straight to the user's keyboard clipboard memory
Deleted immediately before the Subagent can even read them
explanation: All intermediate tool call results of a subagent go only into that subagent's own context window for it to read and analyze, without polluting the Main Context Window at all.

question: Who is responsible for writing the initial `task description` to launch a Subagent when delegating work?
options: The Parent Agent (in the main conversation thread) automatically writes it based on the user's request
The graphics card driver (GPU Driver) randomly generates it
The ISP's DNS system
The Subagent writes the question for itself before being called
explanation: According to Chapter 1: When a subagent is launched, it receives 'A task description written by the parent agent based on what you asked for'.

question: Why does minimizing noise in the Main Context Window help during long Claude Code sessions?
options: The less redundant intermediate data in the main context, the better Claude maintains focus, remembers core instructions longer, and works more effectively throughout long sessions
Because Claude Code only allows running a maximum of 3 commands if Subagents are not used
Because the Main Context Window can only store uppercase English letters
Because it reduces the computer monitor's power consumption by 90%
explanation: 'The less noise in your main context, the longer and more effectively you can work' — keeping the Main Context clean prevents attention dilution and avoids hitting context limits too early.

question: What is a Custom Subagent created specifically to inspect source code quality, find potential bugs, and identify security vulnerabilities commonly called?
options: A code reviewer subagent
A billing manager subagent
A DNS resolver subagent
A hardware overclocking subagent
explanation: Code Reviewer is one of the most classic examples of a Custom Subagent mentioned throughout the course (alongside Test Writer and Documentation Generator).

question: Which of the following statements is FALSE about how Subagents work?
options: Subagents share 100% of the Context Window memory with the Main Conversation, so every file a Subagent reads bloats the Main Context
Each Subagent runs in its own independent Context Window
A Subagent returns a concise summary to the main conversation thread upon completion
Claude Code includes both Built-in Subagents and the ability to create Custom Subagents
explanation: The first statement is FALSE because the most fundamental point of a Subagent is running in an INDEPENDENT Context Window so that it does NOT bloat the Main Context.

question: In Lab 01 (`subagent_context_isolation.py`), when comparing reading 15 files directly in the Main Context versus delegating to an `Explore` Subagent, what do the measurements show?
options: The Main Context using the `Explore` Subagent contains only 2 messages (Question + Result Summary), reducing noisy tokens by over 95% compared to reading 15 files directly in the main thread
The Main Context using a Subagent becomes twice as large as without using a Subagent
Both approaches store all 15 files in the Main Context with the exact same token count
The `Explore` Subagent fails to find the file `src/auth/security.py`
explanation: In Lab 01, isolating 15 `Read` calls into the Subagent Context allows the Main Context to retain only the question and final summary, eliminating over 95% of intermediate tokens from the main thread.

question: When can you start using the Built-in Subagents (`General-purpose`, `Explore`, `Plan`) in Claude Code?
options: Right away, because they are already built into Claude Code without needing to create any configuration files
Only after you manually write at least 10 YAML configuration files in the project directory
Only after you install a local PostgreSQL database on your machine
Only after you recompile Claude Code's source code from scratch
explanation: 'Claude Code ships with several built-in subagents you can use right away' — you can use the 3 built-in subagents immediately with no extra configuration required.

question: In what file format are Custom Subagents in Claude Code stored?
options: Markdown files (`.md`) with YAML Frontmatter at the top holding configuration and a body below containing the System Prompt
Encrypted executable binary files (`.exe` or `.dll`)
Microsoft Excel spreadsheets (`.xlsx`)
Vector graphics image files (`.svg`)
explanation: According to Chapter 2: 'They are defined as markdown files with YAML frontmatter that holds the configuration and a body that describes how the subagent should behave.'

question: According to Chapter 2, what is the easiest way to create a Custom Subagent in the Claude Code CLI?
options: Use the `/agents` wizard (`the /agents wizard`) and describe what you want so Claude generates the configuration file for you
Write a C++ program to generate binary code for the agent
Directly edit the Windows operating system Registry
Submit a technical support ticket to Anthropic asking them to create the file for you
explanation: The easiest way is to use the `/agents` command in the Claude Code CLI: the interactive wizard guides you through choosing Scope, Tools, Model, Color, and can let Claude automatically generate `name`, `description`, and `system prompt` from your brief description.

question: When creating a Subagent at the `Project-level` scope, in which directory is its configuration file saved?
options: `.claude/agents/` (inside the root directory of the current project)
`~/.claude/agents/` (in the user's Home directory)
`/etc/claude/system_agents/`
`node_modules/.bin/agents/`
explanation: A Project-level subagent is saved as a `.md` file inside the project's `.claude/agents/` directory and is only available within the current project (and can be committed to Git to share with the team).

question: When you want to create a personal Subagent that can be shared across ALL projects on your computer (`User-level`), where must the configuration file be placed?
options: `~/.claude/agents/` (in the user's Home directory)
`.claude/agents/` (only inside a single project subdirectory)
`/tmp/agents/` (a temporary directory cleared on reboot)
`./tests/fixtures/agents/`
explanation: A User-level subagent is stored at `~/.claude/agents/`, allowing you to share and reuse that subagent across every project on your computer.

question: In the `/agents` wizard, when choosing how to initialize the configuration content after selecting Scope, what does the 'Generate with Claude' (generation wizard) feature do?
options: You simply enter a short description of what you want, and Claude automatically generates the `name`, `description`, and `system prompt` based on that input
It automatically downloads random source code from the Internet without asking you
It deletes all existing subagents in the project
It only changes the font of the Terminal window
explanation: With the `/agents` generation wizard, you just briefly describe the subagent's purpose, and Claude automatically drafts an accurate `name`, `description`, and detailed `system prompt` for you.

question: In the `Customizing Tools` step of the `/agents` wizard, into which 5 categories are the tools grouped?
options: Read-only tools, Edit tools, Execution tools, MCP tools, and Other tools
Audio tools, Video tools, 3D CAD tools, Printing tools, and Gaming tools
SQL tools, NoSQL tools, Graph tools, Vector tools, and Cache tools
Windows tools, Linux tools, macOS tools, iOS tools, and Android tools
explanation: According to Chapter 2 ('Customizing Tools'), the wizard groups tools into 5 clear categories: Read-only tools, Edit tools, Execution tools, MCP tools, and Other tools.

question: Why should you uncheck the `Edit tools` category for a `code-reviewer` subagent?
options: Because a Code Reviewer only needs to read and analyze code; removing Edit permissions prevents the subagent from accidentally modifying your source code during a review
Because if Edit tools are enabled, Claude Code cannot read Markdown files
Because Edit tools turn the subagent's `color` to black
Because Anthropic charges 10x more for every subagent with Edit tools enabled
explanation: 'A code reviewer probably only needs read-only tools. Unchecking edit or execution tools it doesn't need prevents it from modifying code.' — Granting only the necessary tools ensures complete safety.

question: When configuring the `model` field for a Subagent, what are the 4 valid options?
options: `haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, and `inherit`
`gpt-4`, `llama-3`, `mistral`, and `default`
`small`, `medium`, `large`, and `xlarge`
explanation: The four options for a subagent's `model` field in Claude Code are: `haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, or `inherit`.

question: Among the `model` options for a Subagent, when should you choose `haiku`, `sonnet`, or `opus`?
options: `haiku` is best for fast, lightweight tasks; `sonnet` is a good balance between speed and depth; `opus` is best for complex analysis
`haiku` is for the most complex architectural analysis; `opus` is only for ultra-lightweight search tasks
All three models have 100% identical speed and reasoning capability, differing only in name
`sonnet` can only read image files, while `opus` can only read audio files
explanation: According to 'Choosing a Model and Color' in Chapter 2: Haiku is optimized for fast, lightweight tasks; Sonnet balances speed and depth well; Opus is strongest for complex analysis.

question: If a Subagent's `model` field is set to `inherit` (or omitted from the YAML Frontmatter), which model will that Subagent run on?
options: It will automatically use whatever model your main conversation is currently running
It will throw a `ModelNotFoundError` and refuse to launch
It will always force a downgrade to the oldest model from 2021
It will randomly run a different model on every line of code
explanation: `inherit` means inheritance: the subagent uses the exact same model that the main session is using. If you omit the `model:` line in YAML, it also defaults to `inherit`.

question: What is the practical purpose of choosing a `color` field (e.g., `color: orange` or `color: cyan`) for a Subagent?
options: Displays an identifying color in the Terminal/UI so you can quickly tell which subagent is active, which is especially helpful when multiple subagents are running
Determines the OS CPU scheduling priority (red runs faster than blue)
Changes the background color of all source code files in the project
Requires `color: orange` for the subagent to be allowed to call the `Bash` tool
explanation: 'This shows up in the UI so you can quickly tell which subagent is active. It's a small detail, but it helps when you have multiple subagents running.'

question: What is the standard list of 5 configuration fields in the YAML Frontmatter block of a `.claude/agents/<name>.md` file introduced in Chapter 2?
options: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, and `color`
`id`, `password`, `port`, `host`, and `protocol`
`author`, `version`, `license`, `repository`, and `keywords`
`temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `stop_sequences`, and `stream`
explanation: The YAML Frontmatter block of a subagent configuration file consists of 5 basic fields: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, and `color`.

question: What role does the `name` field in a Subagent's YAML Frontmatter play?
options: It is the unique identifier of the subagent, and also the name you use when asking Claude to invoke that specific subagent in a message
It is the password to unlock the configuration file
It is the name of the large language model on Anthropic's server
It is the absolute path to the Python installation directory
explanation: `name` is the unique identifier for the subagent (e.g., `code-reviewer`). You can use this exact name when messaging Claude: 'Ask the code-reviewer subagent to look at...'.

question: When writing the `description` field in a Subagent configuration file's YAML Frontmatter, what technical formatting rule should be kept in mind?
options: It should be written as a single line without newline characters, clearly explaining what the subagent does, when to use it, and optionally including example scenarios
It must be split into at least 20 separate paragraphs with line breaks
It may only contain integer digits from 0 to 9
It must be written in hexadecimal code
explanation: According to 'The Config File' in Chapter 2: `description` tells Claude what the subagent does and when to use it, and note that it is a single line that doesn't include newline characters.

question: What happens if you OMIT the `tools` field in the YAML Frontmatter of a Subagent configuration file?
options: The subagent defaults to getting access to EVERYTHING (all available tools)
The subagent will have access to zero tools (0 tools)
Claude Code will report a YAML syntax error and delete the configuration file
The subagent will only be allowed to use the `Calculator` tool
explanation: This is a critical detail in Chapter 2: 'tools — Lists which tools the subagent has access to. If you omit this field, the subagent gets access to everything.' Therefore, if you want to restrict permissions, you must explicitly declare the `tools` field!

question: What is the role of the text body located below the YAML Frontmatter (after the second `---` line) in `.claude/agents/<name>.md`?
options: It is the `System Prompt` defining the subagent's role, what it should focus on, how it should make decisions, and how it should report findings back to the Main Agent
It is just human-readable comments that Claude Code completely ignores
It is where error logs from previous runs are stored
It is JavaScript source code used to render the Web UI
explanation: 'The body of the file below the YAML frontmatter is the system prompt. This is where you define the subagent's role, what it should focus on, how it should make decisions, and how it should report findings back to the main agent.'

question: If you want Claude Code to AUTOMATICALLY delegate tasks to your Subagent without you having to explicitly name it each time (`Making Claude Use Your Subagent Automatically`), which keyword should you include in the `description` field?
options: The keyword `"proactively"` (e.g., `"Use this agent proactively when..."`)
The keyword `"sudo_force_run"`
The keyword `"always_block_main_thread"`
The keyword `"disable_context_isolation"`
explanation: According to the final section of Chapter 2 ('Making Claude Use Your Subagent Automatically'): 'If you want Claude to delegate tasks to the subagent without you explicitly asking, include the word "proactively" in the description field.'

question: Besides adding the keyword `"proactively"`, what else can you add to the `description` field to help Claude better recognize real-world situations that should trigger the Subagent?
options: Include example conversations/scenarios in `description` to illustrate what the user might say when the subagent should be called
Attach a `.bmp` screenshot file inside the `description` line
Write the computer's local IP address in `description`
Repeat the subagent's name 50 times in a row
explanation: You can include short example conversations in `description` to guide Claude in accurately recognizing which contexts require automatically invoking the subagent.

question: Can you edit a Subagent configuration file in `.claude/agents/` with a regular text editor (like VS Code) after it has been created by `/agents`?
options: YES — because they are just plain Markdown (`.md`) files, you can open, edit, or version-control them with Git at any time
NO — files created by `/agents` are locked with a digital signature and cannot be manually edited
Only if you delete the entire project and reinstall the operating system
You must use paid third-party specialized software to open `.md` files
explanation: Since subagent config files are just plain Markdown text with YAML Frontmatter at `.claude/agents/*.md`, you can create them from scratch, edit them directly in an IDE, or use `/agents`.

question: What is the main difference when deciding between `Project-level` (`.claude/agents/`) versus `User-level` (`~/.claude/agents/`)?
options: `Project-level` is tied to a specific project (and can be shared with teammates via Git), whereas `User-level` is for personal assistants you want to carry across all projects on your machine
`Project-level` only allows the Haiku model, whereas `User-level` allows the Opus model
`Project-level` does not support restricting `tools`, whereas `User-level` does
`User-level` runs 5x faster than `Project-level` on the same question
explanation: Project-level (`.claude/agents/`) is scoped only to the current project, ideal for repo-specific standards and committing to Git; User-level (`~/.claude/agents/`) is scoped globally to your personal machine for reuse across all projects.

question: According to `How Subagent Config Data Gets Used` (Chapter 3), when you send a message in the Main Context Window, which part of available Subagents' data is loaded into the Main Agent's System Prompt?
options: Only the `name` and `description` of every available Subagent are included in the Main Agent's System Prompt (each Subagent's System Prompt body is NOT loaded yet)
100% of the thousands-of-lines System Prompt body of every Subagent is stuffed into the Main Context from the start
No Subagent information is loaded until the user types `/init`
Only the `color` and `model` fields are loaded into the Main Agent, while `name` and `description` are hidden
explanation: According to Chapter 3: 'When you send a message in the main context window, the name and description of every available subagent are included in the system prompt... If you create a subagent and never use it in a conversation, only the name and description are in context, not the subagent's system prompt.'

question: What TWO critical roles does a Subagent's `description` field serve for the Main Agent?
options: 1) Helps the Main Agent decide WHEN to invoke that Subagent, and 2) Shapes HOW the Main Agent writes the input prompt delegating work to that Subagent
1) Limits the Subagent's network speed, and 2) Encrypts the transcript file on disk
1) Completely replaces the Subagent's System Prompt, and 2) Automatically installs Python libraries
1) Selects the UI color, and 2) Automatically deletes temporary files after running
explanation: This is a core concept of Chapter 3: `description` not only helps the Main Agent decide *when to invoke* the subagent, but also *shapes how the main agent writes the input prompt* sent to the Subagent.

question: What typically happens when you write an overly vague `description` for `code-reviewer` (for example, just: `"Use this agent to review code changes"`)?
options: The Main Agent doesn't know what specific information to pass, so it often writes a vague input prompt like `"use git diff to find current changes"`, forcing the Subagent to hunt around instead of focusing on the exact files to check
The Main Agent will automatically refuse to call the Subagent and shut down the program
The Subagent will automatically be upgraded to the Opus model for free
Claude Code will automatically rewrite the `description` field on disk without asking you
explanation: If `description` doesn't specify what to pass, the Main Agent sends a generic instruction (such as telling the subagent to run `git diff` itself to find changes), wasting time and reducing accuracy.

question: If you update `code-reviewer`'s `description` to include the instruction: `"You must tell the agent precisely which files you want it to review"`, how will the Main Agent's behavior change when calling this Subagent?
options: The Main Agent will read that instruction and proactively list the exact file paths to review right inside the Input Prompt it sends to the Subagent
The Main Agent will force the user to manually type out the entire source code of those files into the chat box
The Subagent will lose permission to use the `Read` tool
The Main Agent will ignore that sentence because the Main Agent never reads the `description` field
explanation: Because the Main Agent reads `description` to know how to delegate to the Subagent, the instruction 'You must tell the agent precisely which files you want it to review' compels the Main Agent to pass the specific file list into the Subagent's Input Prompt!

question: According to `Defining an Output Format` (Chapter 3), if you do NOT clearly specify an output format in a Subagent's System Prompt, what 2 problems do you commonly encounter with the returned summary?
options: 1) Either too vague (losing important details during summarization), or 2) Too verbose (dumping a huge wall of text that bloats the main context)
1) The summary gets translated into French, 2) The summary gets Base64-encoded
1) The Subagent can never stop running, 2) The config file gets renamed
1) The `Bash` tool gets locked, 2) The model automatically switches to `haiku`
explanation: Without a clear Output Format definition: (1) If too vague, important details are lost when summarizing; (2) If too verbose, it dumps too much text back into the Main Context, defeating the purpose of subagent context isolation.

question: In the standard 6-section `Structured Output Format` template for a `code-reviewer` subagent in Chapter 3, into what 3 severity levels are discovered issues categorized?
options: Critical Issues (security, data loss, crashes), Major Issues (logic bugs, missing edge cases, major performance), and Minor Issues (style, naming, small optimizations)
Red Issues, Blue Issues, and Green Issues
Frontend Issues, Backend Issues, and Database Issues
Easy Issues, Medium Issues, and Impossible Issues
explanation: The 6 standard sections in the Chapter 3 example are: (1) Summary, (2) Critical issues, (3) Major issues, (4) Minor issues, (5) Positive observations, and (6) Specific recommendations.

question: In the 6-section report structure of the `code-reviewer` subagent in Chapter 3, what are section 5 and section 6?
options: 5) Positive observations (things done well, clean patterns) and 6) Specific recommendations (concrete, actionable steps to fix the code)
5) Git commit history and 6) Author salary estimation
5) Full source code copy and 6) Raw terminal logs
5) List of all npm packages and 6) Operating system version
explanation: Alongside Summary and the 3 issue levels (Critical, Major, Minor), the report template includes 5. Positive observations (acknowledging good patterns to preserve) and 6. Specific recommendations (clear, concrete fix instructions).

question: Why is designing a `Reporting Obstacles` mechanism critically important for a Subagent?
options: Because the Subagent runs in an isolated context; if environment errors, missing libraries, or failed commands aren't included in the returned summary, the main conversation will never learn about them and will repeat those exact failures!
So the Subagent can automatically send error reports to the computer hardware manufacturer
Because without an Obstacles section, YAML Frontmatter will throw a syntax error
So the Subagent automatically shuts down the computer whenever a test fails
explanation: According to Chapter 3 ('Reporting Obstacles'): 'If those obstacles don't make it into the summary it returns, the main conversation never learns about them — which means wasted time and repeated failures.'

question: According to Chapter 3, what are the 4 typical types of obstacles you want a Subagent to include in its report back to the Main Agent?
options: 1) Setup/environment issues, 2) Permission errors, 3) Commands that failed or required special configuration, and 4) Missing dependencies or unavailable test suites
1) Current weather, 2) Stock prices, 3) Cooling fan speed, and 4) Screen brightness
1) Number of comment lines in code, 2) Commit author name, 3) Repo creation date, and 4) README file size
1) Colors of other subagents, 2) Font list, 3) Audio port, and 4) Browser version
explanation: In 'Reporting Obstacles' (Chapter 3), the 4 groups of obstacle information to report back are: Setup issues or environment problems; Permission errors encountered during the task; Commands that failed or required special configuration; Missing dependencies or unavailable test suites.

question: What is the simplest and most effective way to ensure a Subagent always reports back any obstacles or special configuration flags it encountered during its work?
options: Add a dedicated section such as `"Obstacles Encountered"` to the Output Format specification in the Subagent's System Prompt, instructing it to note any setup errors, permission issues, or commands needing special flags
Set `temperature = 1.0` for the Subagent
Grant full `Edit` and `Write` permissions to every Subagent
Change the Subagent's color to red (`color: red`)
explanation: According to Chapter 3: 'The way to get this information back is to ask for it in the system prompt. Adding an "Obstacles Encountered" section to your output format gives the subagent a dedicated place to report these issues.'

question: According to `Limiting Tool Access` (Chapter 3), granting each Subagent only the tools it actually needs provides what 2 direct benefits?
options: 1) Prevents unintended actions, and 2) Makes each Subagent more focused when it has fewer tool options
1) Doubles the Context Window size, and 2) Automatically enables Prompt Caching
1) Allows running without an API Key, and 2) Automatically generates PDF files
1) Completely eliminates network latency, and 2) Automatically commits code to GitHub
explanation: Chapter 3 explicitly states: 'This does two things: it prevents unintended actions, and it makes each subagent more focused when it has fewer options.'

question: For a `Research or read-only subagent`, what is the standard toolset that should be granted in the `tools` field?
options: Only `Glob`, `Grep`, and `Read` (cannot accidentally modify any files)
Grant `Edit`, `Write`, and `Bash`
Grant only the `Write` tool
Omit the `tools` field so it has access to all tools
explanation: According to 'Limiting Tool Access' in Chapter 3: 'Research or read-only subagent — Only needs Glob, Grep, and Read. Cannot accidentally modify files.'

question: According to Chapter 3 guidelines, what should the standard toolset for a `Code reviewer` subagent include and exclude?
options: Grant `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` plus `Bash` (to run `git diff` and see what changed), but do NOT grant `Edit` or `Write`
Grant `Edit` and `Write` to automatically rewrite all code, but forbid `Read`
Grant only `Bash` and forbid all `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`
Grant no tools at all
explanation: According to Chapter 3: 'Code reviewer — Needs Read access plus Bash to run git diff and see what changed, but shouldn't need Edit or Write.'

question: Why does a `Testing or documentation subagent` need to be granted `Edit` and `Write` permissions?
options: Because its job inherently requires creating or modifying test files and documentation files (docs)
Because every subagent in Claude Code requires `Edit` and `Write` just to start up
Because `Edit` and `Write` are the only two tools used for reading file contents
So it can delete its own configuration file after finishing
explanation: According to Chapter 3: 'Testing or documentation subagent — Needs the broader set, including Edit and Write access, because its job is to create or modify test files and docs.'

question: In the `Putting It All Together` summary at the end of Chapter 3, an Effective Subagent always exhibits which 4 core characteristics?
options: 1) Specific descriptions, 2) Structured output, 3) Obstacle reporting, and 4) Minimal tool access
1) Maximum tool access, 2) Free-form unformatted output, 3) Vague one-word description, and 4) Always using Opus model
1) Shared context window, 2) Global bash root access, 3) Silent error ignoring, and 4) Nested infinite subagents
1) HTML output only, 2) No system prompt, 3) User-level scope only, and 4) Red UI color
explanation: The 'Putting It All Together' section at the end of Chapter 3 summarizes the 4 characteristics of Effective Subagents: (1) Specific descriptions, (2) Structured output, (3) Obstacle reporting, and (4) Minimal tool access.

question: If you create a new Subagent in `.claude/agents/db-helper.md` with a 2,000-token System Prompt, but in the current conversation you have NEVER invoked `db-helper`, how much context does that Subagent consume in the Main Context Window?
options: It only costs a tiny number of tokens for its `name` and `description` (included in the Main Agent's System Prompt), while the 2,000 tokens of `db-helper`'s System Prompt body are NOT loaded into the Main Context at all
It occupies all 2,000 tokens in the Main Context Window from the very first message
It occupies 4,000 tokens because it is duplicated in both Main Context and Subagent Context
It occupies exactly 0 tokens because neither `name` nor `description` is loaded
explanation: This is a smart context-saving mechanism explained at the start of Chapter 3: When a subagent hasn't been called, only its `name` and `description` sit in the Main Agent's context for routing, while the subagent's 2,000-token System Prompt body is not loaded!

question: Suppose while running `pytest`, a Subagent discovers it needs to pass `--tb=short -q` and set `APP_ENV=test` for the test suite to run. If the Subagent records this in `Obstacles Encountered` in its returned summary, what benefit does the Main Agent gain?
options: The Main Agent immediately learns the working command and resolved environment obstacles, so in subsequent steps of the session it won't stumble over that same error again
The Main Agent will automatically delete the `pytest` suite from the project
The Main Agent will lock the user's command execution permissions
No benefit at all because the Main Agent does not read the Subagent's summary
explanation: When a subagent records commands needing special flags or workarounds in `Obstacles Encountered`, the valuable knowledge it discovered in its isolated context is passed back to the Main Agent so it doesn't have to rediscover it from scratch.

question: You are designing a `citation-researcher` subagent specialized in looking up internal documentation to answer questions for the Main Agent. To ensure the Main Agent always receives verifiable citations, which technique from Chapter 3 should you apply?
options: Explicitly require returning citations in both `description` (to shape task delegation) and the `Structured Output Format` section of the System Prompt (requiring file paths and line numbers for every claim)
Simply name the subagent `citation` and leave the System Prompt completely blank
Grant it `Write` and `Edit` tools so it can modify the original documentation
Skip defining an Output Format so the Subagent can write free-form prose however it likes
explanation: Combining guidance in `description` with an output template featuring a `Key Files & Line References` section in the System Prompt ensures reports returned to the Main Agent always include accurate citations.

question: Why should you NOT write a multi-page `description` field for each Subagent?
options: Because the `description` of ALL available Subagents is always loaded into the Main Agent's System Prompt on every chat turn; overly verbose descriptions across many subagents waste Main Context Window space
Because YAML only allows strings with a maximum length of 5 characters
Because if `description` is longer than 10 words, the Subagent automatically switches to read-only mode
Because the Web browser will block displaying the results
explanation: Because every `name` + `description` is persistently present in the Main Agent's System Prompt, `description` needs to be specific and informative (when to use + what inputs to pass) yet concise on a single line.

question: In Lab 03 (`effective_subagent_design.py`), `validate_tool_permissions` checks a Subagent with role `code_reviewer` that has been granted `['Read', 'Grep', 'Glob', 'Bash', 'Edit', 'Write']`. What will the validation result report?
options: Fails Least Privilege compliance because a `code_reviewer` should only inspect and report issues, not have `Edit` or `Write` permissions that alter source code
Passes perfectly because the more tools a Code Reviewer has, the safer it runs
Reports an error for missing system file deletion tools
Reports an error because a Code Reviewer is not allowed to have the `Read` tool
explanation: Per Chapter 3 design standards, `code-reviewer` should only be granted `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, and `Bash` (for `git diff`), and must never be granted `Edit` or `Write`.

question: What structural characteristic of a task indicates it is the MOST IDEAL candidate to delegate to a Subagent?
options: A large volume of data to read/explore (High Input / High Noise) but a compact, clearly summarizable expected result (Low Output / Concise Summary)
A tiny amount of data to read (just 1 line) requiring 20 back-and-forth turns with the user to edit
A task that only needs to check the system time with a single command
A task requiring 5 subagents to simultaneously overwrite the exact same line of the same source file
explanation: 'High Input / Low Output' tasks (like reading 40 files to find all callers of a function or diagnosing a bug from long logs) are where Subagents shine: keeping all raw data in an isolated context and returning only a concise conclusion to the main thread.

question: Because a Subagent launches in a brand-new Context Window and CANNOT see the prior chat history of the main session, what is the most important principle when delegating work to a Subagent?
options: The delegation prompt (Task Description / Input Prompt) must be completely Self-Contained — clearly stating full context, file paths, goals, and constraints without assuming the Subagent knows what was just discussed in the main session
Always write the shortest possible prompt like `"Do it the way we discussed earlier"`
Never pass file names to the Subagent so it has to guess them
Copy-paste 100% of the entire day's chat history into every Subagent
explanation: Due to Context Isolation, a Subagent has no memory of the ongoing Main Session conversation. A prompt like 'Do it the way we discussed earlier' will fail; thus, delegation prompts must always be complete and self-contained.

question: Why does using an independent Subagent for Code Review / Verification after the Main Agent finishes writing code yield a more objective evaluation than having the Main Agent review its own code?
options: Because the Subagent starts with a fresh Context Window, free from the 'authoring / self-approval bias' from the prior code-writing reasoning in the main thread
Because the Subagent always uses a different programming language than the Main Agent
Because the Main Agent is incapable of reading back a file it just created
Because the Subagent can grade code without even reading the source files
explanation: When an agent both writes and reviews code in the same context, it is prone to confirmation/self-approval bias. A `code-reviewer` subagent running in an isolated context only sees the actual output artifact, resulting in sharper, more objective reviews.

question: When the Main Agent launches 3 Subagents in parallel at the same time (e.g., Subagent A, Subagent B, Subagent C), how do these Subagents communicate with each other?
options: They are completely isolated and CANNOT see what sibling Subagents are doing; each works in its own context and returns a summary report to the Main Agent to synthesize
All 3 Subagents share a group chat window and edit each other's prompts in real time
Subagent A automatically becomes the supervisor of Subagent B and Subagent C
Subagent C must wait for Subagents A and B to shut down the computer before reading files
explanation: Parallel subagents do not share context with one another and cannot see what sibling subagents are doing. All coordination and result synthesis go through the Main Agent (Hub-and-Spoke model).

question: How do you get Claude Code to use multiple Subagents IN PARALLEL to explore a large codebase faster?
options: Explicitly instruct Claude in your prompt to use multiple parallel subagents and assign clearly independent scopes to each branch (e.g., `"Explore this codebase using 3 parallel subagents: one for frontend, one for backend APIs, and one for auth"`)
Type the same question 3 times in a row without mentioning subagents
Open 100 Chrome browser tabs simultaneously on your computer
Set `temperature = 0.0` in the `.env` file
explanation: Claude Code tends to work sequentially and cautiously unless you specify otherwise. Explicitly requesting parallel subagents with disjoint scopes significantly cuts down wall-clock wait time.

question: What is the biggest risk when running multiple Subagents with `Edit` / `Write` permissions IN PARALLEL on the same area of a codebase?
options: Write / Merge Conflicts — because the Subagents are unaware of each other, they will edit the same file simultaneously and overwrite each other's changes!
The Subagents will automatically switch to Read-only mode
The SSD will fill up immediately after 1 second
Claude Code will automatically delete the current Git branch
explanation: Because each subagent runs in an isolated context yet operates on the same physical workspace filesystem, if 2 parallel subagents edit the same file, they cause write conflicts (race conditions / merge conflicts).

question: To avoid conflicts when orchestrating multiple Subagents in parallel, what is the Best Practice?
options: Prioritize parallelism for READ-ONLY tasks (exploration, searching, multi-perspective reviews); if parallel code edits are needed, partition Subagents to work on completely disjoint files/directories
Always grant `Write` permissions to all parallel Subagents and let them fight over file locks
Never run more than 1 Subagent in a single day
Force every parallel Subagent to edit `main.py` at the same time
explanation: Running read-only subagents in parallel (exploration, security audit, code review) is completely safe. If parallel file writes are used, each subagent must own a completely non-overlapping set of files.

question: In which of the following scenarios should you NOT use a Subagent (Anti-Pattern)?
options: When you only need to read or quickly edit 1 small file whose path is already known, or when the task requires continuous back-and-forth iterative refinement with the user across many turns
When you need to scan 50 files in a project to find all usages of a function about to be deprecated
When you want a `code-reviewer` to independently check recently modified files without polluting the main thread
When you need to understand the architecture of 4 large, independent modules at the same time
explanation: For simple single-file tasks or tasks requiring high back-and-forth iteration with the user, spinning up a subagent incurs unnecessary startup overhead and breaks direct conversational flow.

question: What design flaw does the term `"Subagent Sprawl"` refer to?
options: Creating dozens of overly granular micro-subagents with overlapping functions, bloating the Main Agent's System Prompt and confusing the Main Agent when deciding which Subagent to delegate to
Allowing a Subagent to read more than 5 files in a single run
Using the `sonnet` model for a Subagent instead of `haiku`
Storing Subagent configuration files in the `.claude/agents/` directory
explanation: Subagent Sprawl occurs when users create too many unnecessary micro-subagents. Because every `name` + `description` is loaded into the Main Agent, having too many overlapping subagents wastes main context and degrades routing accuracy.

question: Why should you NOT grant nested subagent spawning tools to a regular Subagent?
options: To keep the Subagent as a leaf worker, preventing uncontrolled recursive cascading delegation that explodes token costs and latency
Because Windows only allows opening a maximum of 1 Python process
Because granting it causes Markdown files to lose their display colors
Because Claude Code does not allow the Main Agent to call any Subagent
explanation: Keeping a flat architecture (Main Agent acts as orchestrator calling leaf subagents) maintains tight control over the workflow and prevents subagents from spawning child/grandchild subagents uncontrollably.

question: How does the `Model Tiering` technique optimize cost and speed when using Subagents?
options: Use a capable model (like `opus` or `sonnet`) for the Main Agent to plan and orchestrate, while assigning faster, more economical models (like `haiku` or `sonnet`) in the configs of Subagents dedicated to searching or routine checks
Force every Subagent and the Main Agent to run on the most expensive model for every tiny task
Move all complex architectural planning to `haiku` and use `opus` only to count lines in a file
Turn off AI models completely and switch to manual searching
explanation: Thanks to the `model` field in `.claude/agents/*.md`, you can apply Model Tiering: run high-volume exploration/search subagents on `haiku` (ultra-fast and cheap), review subagents on `sonnet`, and the main session on `opus`/`sonnet`.

question: What is the CORRECT understanding of Token Economics when using Subagents?
options: Subagents are designed to protect the cleanliness and accuracy of the Main Context Window (avoiding re-sending tens of thousands of noisy tokens on every subsequent turn), whereas an individual Subagent call still consumes its own tokens in its own window
All tokens consumed by a Subagent in its own window are 100% free and do not count toward usage limits
Running 10 Subagents in parallel always uses fewer total tokens than reading 1 single file in the main thread
Subagents never use any input tokens at all
explanation: Subagents are not 'free tokens' — each subagent still consumes tokens in its own context. However, they prevent tens of thousands of intermediate tokens from sticking permanently in the Main Context Window, keeping subsequent main-thread turns lean, accurate, and economical long-term.

question: When is using a Subagent as a 'Discardable Sandbox' most effective?
options: When you want to investigate a bug hypothesis or uncertain approach that might hit a dead end — if it fails, all those messy trial logs close with the Subagent without polluting the main conversation
When you already know with 100% certainty that you need to fix line 5 in `README.md`
When you want to permanently delete the company's Git repository
When you just want to ask Claude a theoretical question unrelated to the codebase
explanation: When investigating a complex hypothesis (which might require reading many files and trying multiple paths), delegating to a subagent keeps all dead ends outside the main thread; the Main Context only receives the final verdict on whether that path is viable.

question: You want to review a large Pull Request from 3 deep perspectives: (1) Security vulnerabilities (`security-auditor`), (2) SQL query performance (`perf-reviewer`), and (3) Test coverage (`test-coverage`). What is the most effective way to organize Subagents?
options: Run all 3 specialized Subagents in parallel in Read-only mode on the list of changed files, then have the Main Agent synthesize the 3 structured reports into one unified review
Combine everything into 1 single Subagent with no System Prompt and no Output Format
Grant `Edit` and `Write` to all 3 Subagents so they can directly edit the Pull Request files simultaneously
Force the user to copy each line of code into 3 different computers
explanation: This is the classic 'Multi-Perspective Reviews' pattern: 3 read-only subagents with specialized System Prompts run in parallel simultaneously, each focusing 100% on one angle and returning a structured report for the Main Agent to synthesize.

question: If a task consists of 3 tightly state-dependent sequential steps (Step 2 needs the full detailed reasoning context of Step 1, and Step 3 needs the full details of Step 2), what problem does splitting each step into a separate Subagent cause?
options: Causes Context Fragmentation — because each new Subagent only receives a condensed summary rather than the full detailed reasoning chain of the previous step, leading to loss of important information between steps
Makes all 3 steps run simultaneously 3x faster
Allows the Subagents to automatically share RAM with each other
Automatically merges the 3 `.md` config files into 1 single file
explanation: Subagents are built for self-contained tasks that only need to return a summary. For a chain of steps requiring continuous detailed state continuity, slicing them into sequential subagents drops context at every summarization boundary.

question: When a Subagent hits a hard blocker such as a missing `.env` config file or lack of access permissions to a target directory, what is the most appropriate behavior to design into the Subagent?
options: Stop guessing, record the exact nature of the blocker, what was tried, and what is missing in `Obstacles Encountered`, and immediately return control to the Main Agent to handle
Keep retrying the exact same failing command 500 times in an infinite loop
Automatically hallucinate fake data and report to the Main Agent that everything succeeded 100%
Automatically create fake config files with random passwords and overwrite the system
explanation: Instead of looping endlessly or fabricating results when hitting a hard blocker in an isolated context, the Subagent must report honestly in `Obstacles Encountered` and return control early so the Main Agent or user can provide the missing information.

question: What is the Rule of Thumb for quickly checking whether a job is suitable to delegate to a Subagent?
options: If you can describe the task completely in a short, self-contained paragraph and expect back a concise, synthesized answer after it reads lots of data on its own, delegate it to a Subagent!
Only delegate tasks that cannot be expressed in words and require asking the user every 5 seconds
Every question under 3 letters must be delegated to a Subagent
Only delegate when you don't want any summary returned
explanation: A task with a clear self-contained brief as input, heavy/multi-step processing in the middle, and a concise synthesis as output is the ideal profile for Subagent delegation.

question: When designing a Subagent system for a team project on Git, where should you store standardized project Subagents (like `code-reviewer`, `test-writer`) and how should they be configured?
options: Store at Project-level (`.claude/agents/*.md`), include `proactively` and clear input parameter instructions in `description`, specify `Structured Output` with an `Obstacles Encountered` section, and restrict `tools` to the minimum needed
Store in the personal `/tmp/` folder, omit `tools`, and write no System Prompt
Store them all inside `.gitignore` so no one on the team can use them
Write instructions for all 20 subagents on a single line inside `package.json`
explanation: Placing them in `.claude/agents/*.md` shares them across the team via Git, and combining all 4 design pillars (Specific description + Proactively, Structured output, Obstacle reporting, Minimal tool access) yields the highest-quality Subagent suite.

question: In Lab 04 (`orchestrating_subagents.py`), when `evaluate_delegation_decision` evaluates the scenario: `'Run 3 subagents in parallel to directly edit app.py at the same time'`, what decision does the system make?
options: Rejects parallel Subagents (`use_subagent: False`) with a `Write Conflict Risk` warning — multiple parallel subagents editing the same file will cause write conflicts!
Recommends immediately running 10 subagents writing to `app.py` to type code faster
Automatically deletes `app.py` to avoid conflicts
Switches all 3 subagents to the `opus` model so they can negotiate with each other
explanation: Lab 04 clearly illustrates the safety rule for parallelism: never allow multiple parallel subagents to write/edit the exact same file simultaneously (`parallel_shared_file_writes`).

question: Course Summary for *Introduction to Subagents*: What is the complete formula combining all 4 Chapters to master Subagents in Claude Code?
options: Understand Context Isolation & Summary Return (Ch. 1) -> Create `.claude/agents/*.md` with `/agents`, choose Model/Tools/Color & `proactively` (Ch. 2) -> Write input-shaping `description`, `Structured Output`, `Obstacles Encountered` & `Least Privilege Tools` (Ch. 3) -> Self-contained delegation for High-Input/Low-Output tasks or safe parallelism (Ch. 4)
Always disable all Built-in Subagents -> Omit `tools` for full permissions -> Never define Output Format -> Create 50 subagents for every simple 1-file read
Use only a single Main Context Window for everything and never use `/agents`
Delegate all continuous back-and-forth user dialogue to a Subagent and delete transcript files after every run
explanation: This option encompasses the entire learning arc across all 4 chapters of Anthropic Academy's *Introduction to Subagents* course!
